The Lows and Clip buttons offer quick adjustments of the circuits most oft tweaked parameters. With the buttons up the circuit is a more traditional voiced TS style drive. While not straying too far from what makes that original design so magical, the Envy expands the range of the controls and offers players more flexibility in getting their own sound. The Level control has been tuned for better output while the Drive control has been altered to allow for less gain at minimum and more gain at maximum. The voicing of the unit has been tuned for a slightly fuller tone. What makes the Envy so special are the two Push Buttons, a first for Mythos. When in the up position, it's the classic TS style sound. Engaging the LOWS push button allows you fatten up the low end for a more even sound that's slightly less mid forward. With the CLIP button in the up position, it's the stock Silicon Soft Clipping we all know, but when you push the button in it removes the diodes from the circuit. Removing the diodes makes the pedal much louder but also you're getting all the character of the op amp, for a more open and dynamic sound. A far cry from the compressed clipping of the stock diodes, but the 4 different combinations this affords you allows for a wide variety of sounds. Internally the Envy features a socketed RC4558P chip, one of the iconic chips we've read about in so many forums and product listings. Mythos has opted to make this socketed so the adventurous user may easily swap the chip out with any similar dual op amp and truly make this pedal their own. Zach from Mythos is known far and wide as a fan of this circuit, we didn't choose to reinvent the wheel but give players the best take we could on such an iconic overdrive pedal. sources.description: OKKO FX Holy Grit: a versatile fuzz face and tonebender based dirt box that feels like an amp-in-a-box, spanning boost, breakup and cranked tweed fuzz.
sources.snippet: OKKO FX Holy Grit Demo Review | Loopy Demos
sources.bodyExcerpt: --> OKKO FX Holy Grit Demo Review | Loopy Demos Show or hide the side bar navigation Loopy Demos Demos Posts Manufacturers About Contact Demos Posts Manufacturers About Contact All demos OKKO FX Holy Grit Jun 1, 2022 Read next Budget Guitar Pedals That Sound Expensive: Best Value Effects Under $150 The Holy Grit by OKKO FX is a Fuzz Face/Tone Bender-inspired dirt box that refuses to stay in one lane. Built by hand in Leipzig since 2003, it runs from a clean boost all the way through woody breakup and into full-on cranked-tweed fuzz. The circuit uses matched low-gain silicon transistors, and the result sits closer to an overdriven amp than a pedal clanging against a clean signal. I kept reaching for it when I wanted body and character rather than just a blanket of gain. Controls The panel puts Fuzz and Level in the top row, with Bass and Treble below flanking a centre Bias toggle. That toggle is the personality control: up is high headroom, clean and precise; middle is slightly underbiased, buzzy and hairy; down is medium gain, a bit thicker. In the demo I’ve set up sweeps for the Fuzz Knob, Bass Knob, Treble Knob, and Bias Toggle so you can hear what each one does. Bass is a pre-gain control, so dialing it up pushes more signal into the gain stage and raises the fuzz intensity. Treble is post-gain, rolling off brightness after the dirt happens. Neither has a huge range, which I think is intentional. You can’t really dial in a bad sound. Level has a lot of headroom, with unity around 10 o’clock, leaving the upper half for clean boosting or front-end smashing. A buffer toggle on the top face lets you place the pedal anywhere in a chain without the usual fuzz-face impedance headaches. Everything here was recorded buffered, since unbuffered mode needs real pickups at the input, which my reamping setup can’t replicate. How It Sounds The Cranked Tweed preset is the most characterful spot on the pedal: Fuzz maxed, Bias in the middle position. The whole thing gets that loose, harmonically complex voice of a tweed amp hitting its limits, which is the preset I kept coming back to for Neil Young-ish open chords. Light Breakup pulls back the Fuzz and lifts the Bias to the high-headroom position. The grit thins out to something closer to a slightly pushed amp, still defined and responsive. Sweet Fuzz goes the other direction: Fuzz and Bass both maxed, Bias in the low position. That stacks the pre-gain bass boost against the lower bias and you get into properly saturated fuzz territory. The Boost preset zeroes the Fuzz knob entirely and cranks Level and Treble. With Fuzz at zero the circuit runs nearly clean and the output becomes a bright, punchy boost. It also works well on bass, where the pre-gain Bass control and amp-like voicing translate without getting woolly. Holy Grit vs Keeley Fuzz Bender Both pedals are rooted in Tone Bender topology and both offer more flexibility than a classic two-knob fuzz. The Keeley Fuzz Bender adds a three-band EQ and a dry Blend control, which makes it easier to dial in extreme gated velcro sounds while keeping low-end definition. The Holy Grit has no dry blend, but the Bias toggle and pre-gain Bass control let you shape the character of the saturation itself rather than sculpting around it. The Fuzz Bender leans more modern and surgical; the Holy Grit leans more analog and amp-like. Who It’s For Players who love the idea of a fuzz but find most fuzzes too one-dimensional will get a lot out of this. The Alpha Haunt by Old Blood Noise Endeavors is the expanded version of the Haunt Fuzz: a silicon high-gain gated fuzz that layers on a 3-band EQ, a parallel Enhance boost, and three extra toggle switches. The result is a gated, velcro-textured fuzz that you can sculpt pretty precisely to fit any rig, from a tight and squeezed splat to a loose, grinding wall of sound. I was very drawn to the Haunt and Alpha Haunt because of its gated texture. Because, as you might know, I love velcro fuzz . With all the extra EQ and gain staging controls, it’s very easy to find a sound that fits your taste and setup. Controls The panel splits into three zones. On the left: Fuzz (gain), Gate (compression and fuzz amount), and Tone (main voice). In the center: three horizontal toggles across the top (Bias, Distortion, LPF), followed by three vertical EQ sliders (Low, Mid, High). On the right: Fuzz Vol (the fuzz section’s output level), Master (overall volume), and Enhance (a blendable boost that folds in unprocessed signal in parallel with the fuzz). The three toggles are where the character shifts. The Bias toggle changes the gating character of the fuzz. The Distortion toggle sets the fuzz range. The LPF toggle adjusts the tone range. In the demo above I’ve set up sweeps for the Fuzz, Gate, Enhance, Bias, Distortion, and LPF controls, so you can hear exactly what each one does to the same riff. I’m especially a fan of the 3-band EQ. With the Mid slider, you can dial in a characterful midrange that cuts through a mix, boost Low for extra weight, or pull High back to tame the top end. How It Sounds No matter how you set the fuzz controls, the texture always seems satisfyingly velcro-y. Squeezed Fuzz in the demo demonstrates this with Gate at 7 and a noticeable compression on the attack. Classic Velcro Fuzz pushes Fuzz to 8 and Fuzz Vol to 10 for a more open, ripping sound. Happy Buzzing sets Gate to 0 entirely, which loosens the gating and lets the fuzz breathe and buzz more freely. Mids and Character cranks Enhance to 10 and Mid to 10, which shows just how much the parallel boost and the EQ can reshape the overall voice without touching the core fuzz sound. The range from smooth overdrive to crumbling gated fuzz is genuinely wide here. The Gate knob sweep in the demo goes from fully open to hard gating, which is the single most dramatic control on the board. Alpha Haunt vs Pardner Fuzz Both are OBNE fuzzes with more than the usual controls, but they approach the brief differently. The Pardner Fuzz centers on its Lasso FX loop: an overdriven effects loop you can run in series or parallel with the fuzz, switchable between a synthy and a fuzzy voice. Its main appeal is routing flexibility and experimental texture. The Alpha Haunt does not have an FX loop or a synth mode. What it has instead is deeper gain staging, a dedicated 3-band EQ, and the Enhance circuit for blending in the clean signal. If you want to shape a gated velcro fuzz sound with precision and you plan to stack it with existing pedals rather than routing effects through it, the Alpha Haunt is the better fit. If the Lasso loop concept is the draw, the Pardner is the one to look at. There’s also a side by side page for this one: Keeley Fuzz Bender vs Old Blood Noise Endeavors Alpha Haunt , both pedals on the same loop so you can switch between them mid-phrase. Who It’s For Players who specifically want a gated, velcro-style fuzz with serious tonal control get the most out of this. The 3-band EQ and Enhance knob make it easier to dial in than a simpler gated fuzz, so it works well if you’re running a bright amp or a dark amp and need to compensate. sources.bodyExcerpt: Old Blood Noise Endeavors Presents The Alpha Haunt Fuzz: A Deep Technical and Sonic Review | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / gear reviews gear reviews Old Blood Noise Endeavors Presents The Alpha Haunt Fuzz: A Deep Technical and Sonic Review By Liam Carter July 19, 2026 Old Blood Noise Endeavors’ Alpha Haunt Fuzz is not just another boutique fuzz pedal — it’s a paradigm shift in analog distortion design. Released in late 2023, this 4.5" × 3.75" × 2.1" (114 × 95 × 53 mm), hand-wired, true-bypass stompbox features two independent, cascaded fuzz engines — one germanium-based, one silicon-based — each with dedicated gain, tone, and volume controls, plus a third global 'Haunt' control that modulates low-end resonance and harmonic decay. Unlike most dual-fuzz pedals, the Alpha Haunt allows simultaneous or serial blending, offers selectable input impedance (1MΩ or 100kΩ via internal DIP switch), and maintains DC-coupled signal integrity across both stages. Measured THD at unity output sits at 12.8% with germanium alone, 21.4% with silicon alone, and peaks at 36.7% when both are engaged at mid-gain settings — significantly higher than a vintage Dallas Arbiter Fuzz Face (≈9.2%) or Electro-Harmonix Big Muff Pi (≈18.1%). This review documents extensive bench testing, live rig integration, and sonic profiling across multiple instruments and amplifiers. The Genesis of a Dual-Engine Design Old Blood Noise Endeavors (OBNE), founded by guitarist and circuit designer Josh Holley in Portland, Oregon, has built its reputation on unconventional topology and expressive modulation — from the Afterglow delay to the Minim reverb. The Alpha Haunt emerged from Holley’s frustration with traditional fuzz limitations: narrow dynamic response, high-frequency roll-off under gain stacking, and inconsistent interaction with passive pickups. Rather than layering effects digitally or using op-amp-based fuzz emulation, OBNE committed to discrete, transistor-level fidelity. The Alpha Haunt’s core innovation lies in its separation of gain generation into two physically distinct circuits sharing only the final output buffer and power regulation stage. The germanium engine uses matched OC44 transistors (selected for h FE between 110–135 at 1mA, verified with a Peak Atlas SMT100 tester) biased at 1.8V collector-emitter voltage. Its input stage employs a 1MΩ pulldown resistor and a 100nF film coupling cap, preserving low-end transient response far better than vintage Fuzz Face designs (which use 10nF). The silicon engine centers on BC549C transistors (h FE 420–500, measured at 2mA), running at 4.2V V CE , with a 470pF ceramic high-frequency peaking cap in the feedback loop — a deliberate nod to the tonal aggression of the Pro Co Rat’s LM308 op-amp, but implemented discretely. Component-Level Rigor Every Alpha Haunt undergoes component binning: carbon-film resistors (±5%) for thermal stability, polypropylene film caps (WIMA MKS2 series) for phase linearity, and hand-soldered 22-gauge tinned copper wire for internal connections. Power regulation is handled by a discrete 9V LDO (MIC5205-3.3YM5) feeding both engines independently, eliminating cross-stage noise coupling — a common flaw in multi-stage pedals like the Fulltone OCD v2. Claim News Orange Amplification Launch Fur Coat and Getaway Driver Pedals The Fur Coat is a vintage fuzz and the Getaway Driver is an overdrive, cab sim, class A type pedal. by Guitar.com August 25, 2017 by Guitar.com August 25, 2017 When you purchase through affiliate links on Guitar.com, you may contribute to our site through commissions. Learn more Want more news stories from Guitar.com ? Follow us on Google News. The Fur Coat, inspired by the great fuzz tones from the seventies is loosely based on the old Foxx Tone Machine originally released in 1971 which was often used by artists such as Peter Frampton and Adrian Belew. Designed with a foot switchable octave, it is superbly versatile, allowing players to adjust the level of the upper octave rather than just turn it on and off. In keeping with the era’s vibe, it is built with germanium diodes and is Orange’s only true bypass pedal. When used it puts a ‘dirty, smelly fur coat’ on every note produced giving them a warm, furry quality. The Fur Coat drapes itself over the music; stroke it lovingly to produce grungy, warm effects or turn it up for lots of filthy, shaggy texture. Its tone can be dressed down casual, super modern, funky or wonderfully dramatic. ‘It sounds absolutely phenomenal’ said Clutch’s Tim Sult and Matt Pike from Sleep said “I’ve tried every fuzz pedal on the planet. This is my new favorite. The Fur Coat is everything I expected Orange would do with an octave fuzz. It’s seriously gnarly.” The action-packed Getaway Driver is an amp-in-a-box type pedal. It has the same transparent, buffered output as the Orange Two Stroke and Kongpressor pedals plus a second Cab Sim / headphone output. This makes the Getaway Driver perfect for silent practice or recording. The three dials, Volume, Bite (tone) and Gain, allow players to ‘rev their engine’. The pedal really excels when played through an amp’s clean channel, even ones with a bright cap. Low gain and high volume makes for a clean boost, pushing amps over the edge into classic overdrive. Armed with one of these, players can be transported back to the fast and furious seventies feeling the heat as this hot rod pedal drives relentlessly forward to produce the closest thing to the buzz of being a real getaway driver. ‘This pedal is great……..it sounds like vintage Orange’ observed Damon Fox The Cult/ Big Elf. The Fur Coat can be powered by 9 or 12V DC. Running at 12V increases the headroom and the output volume available. It draws very little current, less than 5mA allowing for a long battery life. The Getaway Driver can be powered by 9 or 12V DC. At 9Vs the pedal has the characteristics of EL84 valves, whereas 12Vs gives it a EL34 flavour.
